title: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
summary: How LLM pretraining runs its GEMMs in 8 and 4 bits: FP8 formats and scaling, DeepSeek-V3's recipe, FP8 communication and optimizer state, outliers and debugging, MX and NVFP4, and a fake quantizer you build.
outcomes: Explain what E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1 can represent and why range and precision trade off
Compute a scale factor from amax and predict underflow, rounding and saturation after casting
Explain why fine-grained tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion made DeepSeek-V3's FP8 training work
Estimate step speedup and bytes per parameter when FP8 reaches gradients, optimizer state and communication
Trace outliers to massive activations and SwiGLU alignment, and debug a diverging low-precision run
Compare MXFP4 and NVFP4 block scaling on a worked block and compute their storage cost
Build a NumPy fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4 and measure its error on any tensor
Justify each part of the NVFP4 training recipe and compare it with other FP4 training recipes

lessons.title: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1

blocks.md:
Most of the compute in training a transformer is in the matrix multiplies (GEMMs) of its linear layers. Tensor cores (the parts of a GPU built for matrix math) run narrower inputs faster: the DeepSeek-V3 report notes that moving those GEMMs from BF16 (a 16-bit float with the same range as a 32-bit float but far fewer precision bits; the name stands for brain floating point, from Google Brain) to FP8 *theoretically doubles* their speed, and NVIDIA lists Blackwell tensor cores at 2x BF16 throughput for MXFP8 and 4x (GB200) or 6x (GB300) for 4-bit NVFP4. Blackwell is NVIDIA's GPU generation after Hopper (the H100 family), GB200 and GB300 are its data-center parts, and MXFP8 and NVFP4 are block-scaled 8-bit and 4-bit formats taught in lessons 5 and 7. Narrower numbers can also halve the memory and bandwidth for activations saved for the backward pass, if those are kept in FP8 too (lesson 4).

The catch is that 8 or 4 bits can hold very few distinct values. This course is about the tricks that make training work anyway.

A quick recall of **mixed precision training** (Micikevicius et al., 2017), which this all builds on: the forward and backward math runs in a 16-bit format while an FP32 *master copy* of the weights receives the updates (a small update added to a 16-bit weight would round away). With FP16 (IEEE half precision) you also need **loss scaling**: the smallest positive FP16 value is about $6 \times 10^{-8}$ ($2^{-24}$), so gradients much smaller than that round to zero. The fix is to multiply the loss by a constant, which by the chain rule multiplies every gradient by the same constant, so tiny gradients do not round to zero, then divide it back out before the update. BF16 has FP32's range, so it usually needs no loss scaling.

FP8 and FP4 training push the same idea further: only the inputs of the big GEMMs go narrow, everything else stays in BF16 or FP32.

A binary float has three fields: a **sign** bit S, an **exponent** field E (stored with a fixed offset called the *bias*) and a **mantissa** M of m bits (the fraction after an implied leading 1). The name says the split: **E4M3** has 4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits, **E5M2** has 5 and 2, and the 4-bit **E2M1** has 2 and 1. With e exponent bits the bias is $2^{e-1} - 1$ (7 for 4 bits, 15 for 5, 1 for 2), which centers the stored exponents around zero so about half are negative. The values from one power of two up to the next form a *binade*, and every binade holds the same $2^m$ mantissa values. When E is all zeros the number is *subnormal*: the implied 1 is dropped, which lets values fade gradually toward zero.

In the same notation FP32 is E8M23, FP16 is E5M10 and BF16 is E8M7: BF16 keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits, and so its range. IEEE 754, the standard that defines FP32 and FP16, reserves the all-ones exponent for infinity and NaN.

blocks.caption: In words: a normal value is the sign, times 2 to the power (E minus bias), times (1 plus M over 2 to the power m). A subnormal uses exponent 1 minus bias and drops the 1. E4M3 uses bias 7 and m = 3. E5M2 uses bias 15 and m = 2. E2M1 uses bias 1 and m = 1.

blocks.title: Decoding E4M3 bit patterns

scenes.caption: E = 0111 is 7, minus the bias 7 gives exponent 0. M = 000 gives fraction 1.0. So the pattern encodes 1.0.
3.5 is 1.75 x 2^1. Exponent 1 is stored as 1 + 7 = 8 (1000), and 0.75 = 6/8 is stored as M = 110.
The largest E4M3 value: E = 1111 and M = 110 give 1.75 x 2^8 = 448. E4M3 gives up infinities so this top binade holds ordinary numbers.
S.1111.111 is the only NaN pattern in E4M3. Without this trick the maximum would be 240, as in an IEEE-style 4-bit exponent.
The smallest positive E4M3 value is the subnormal 0.0000.001 = 2^-9, about 0.00195. Anything below half of that rounds to zero.

blocks.md:
The FP8 paper by NVIDIA, Arm and Intel (Micikevicius et al., 2022) defines both 8-bit encodings:

- **E4M3**: max 448, min normal $2^{-6}$, min subnormal $2^{-9}$, about 18 binades of range. No infinities, one NaN pattern.
- **E5M2**: max 57,344, min normal $2^{-14}$, min subnormal $2^{-16}$, about 32 binades. Follows IEEE conventions, like FP16 with fewer mantissa bits.

The range in binades counts the doublings from the smallest subnormal up to the max, $\log_2(\text{max}) - \log_2(\text{min})$: $\log_2 448 + 9 \approx 17.8$ for E4M3 and $\log_2 57344 + 16 \approx 31.8$ for E5M2. Casting rounds each value to the nearest representable value; an exact tie goes to the neighbour whose last mantissa bit is 0 (*round-to-nearest-even*), so ties do not all drift the same way.

The paper recommends E4M3 for weights and activations and E5M2 for gradients. The 4-bit **E2M1** element format used by MXFP4 and NVFP4 can only hold 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6 (and their negatives): 3.58 binades from 0.5 to 6.

blocks.prompt: E4M3 has 3 mantissa bits. Between 256 and 448 the representable values are 256, 288, 320, ... What does 300 become in E4M3, and in E5M2?
blocks.reveal:
In E4M3 the step in the binade [256, 512) is $2^{8-3} = 32$, so the neighbours of 300 are 288 and 320, and 300 rounds to **288** (error 12). In E5M2 the step is $2^{8-2} = 64$, the neighbours are 256 and 320, and 300 rounds to **320** (error 20).

Every binade holds the same number of values, so the step doubles with each power of two. The *relative* error stays roughly constant: the step is $2^{-m}$ times the binade's lowest value and rounding moves a value by at most half a step, so at most $2^{-4}$, which is 6.25%, for E4M3 and $2^{-3}$, which is 12.5%, for E5M2 in the normal range.

blocks.title: Relative gap between neighbouring values

scenes.caption: E4M3: in its normal range the gap to the next value is 6.25% to 12.5% of the value (a sawtooth, one tooth per binade). Below 2^-6 it is subnormal and the relative gap explodes.
E5M2 is twice as coarse (12.5% to 25%) but its normal range reaches down to 2^-14 and up to 57,344: one more exponent bit buys about 14 more binades.
The tradeoff in one picture: exponent bits buy range, mantissa bits buy precision. Neither format covers what a raw gradient tensor needs on its own, which is why scaling (next lesson) is essential.

blocks.md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

"FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision. Lesson 4 shows what that means for memory and speed, and the recipes that push FP8 into communication and optimizer state too.

blocks.question: A value of 0.2 is cast to E2M1 (FP4) with no scale factor. What is stored?
options: 0.2 exactly
0.5, the smallest positive FP4 value
0, because 0.2 is below the halfway point 0.25 between 0 and 0.5
6, because out-of-range values saturate
blocks.explain: E2M1's smallest positive value is the subnormal 0.5. Round-to-nearest sends anything below 0.25 to 0, so 0.2 underflows. FP4 is useless without a per-block scale that first stretches values into its tiny 0.5 to 6 window.

blocks.question: Without any scaling, which tensor type gains the most from E5M2 instead of E4M3?
options: Weights, because they are updated every step
Activations after LayerNorm, because they are near 1
Gradients, because their magnitudes spread over many more binades
None: both formats have the same range
blocks.explain: Gradients span a wide range of small magnitudes, so the extra exponent bit (about 32 binades instead of 18) matters most there. That is why the FP8 paper recommends E5M2 for gradients and E4M3 for weights and activations.

lessons.title: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window

blocks.md: Weight gradients in a large model are often tiny. Take eight gradient values between $9 \times 10^{-5}$ and $5.1 \times 10^{-3}$. E4M3's smallest positive value is $2^{-9} \approx 0.00195$, so cast directly, 4 of the eight become exactly zero and the rest snap to one of a few coarse subnormal values. The information is gone before the GEMM even starts.

The fix is the same idea as loss scaling, applied per tensor. Before casting, multiply by a **scale factor** $s$ chosen so the tensor's largest magnitude (its **amax**) lands at the format's maximum. After the GEMM, divide the output by the product of the two input scales. The FP8 paper notes that this un-scaling happens once per dot product, so its cost is amortized over thousands of multiply-adds.

blocks.tex: s = \frac{\text{FP8\_MAX}}{\text{amax}(x)}, \qquad x_q = \text{cast}(s \cdot x), \qquad A B \approx \frac{A_q B_q}{s_A \, s_B}
blocks.caption: Why divide by both scales: the quantized A is about A times its scale and the quantized B is about B times its scale, so their product is about AB times both scales. FP8_MAX is 448 for E4M3 and 57,344 for E5M2. Values that still exceed the range saturate to the maximum.

blocks.title: Scaling eight gradient values into E4M3 (units of 1e-4)

scenes.caption: The true gradients, written in units of 1e-4 so they fit. The amax is 51e-4 = 0.0051 (index 4).
Cast straight to E4M3: four values underflow to 0 and the others snap to multiples of 2^-9 (19.5e-4). Relative errors range from 15% to 100%.
Now multiply by s = 448 / 0.0051 = 87,843 first. The amax lands exactly on 448 and every value sits in E4M3's normal range.
Round to E4M3. Above 256 the step is 32 (so -298.7 becomes -288); between 32 and 64 it is 4 (so 53.6 becomes 52).
Divide by s to decode. Every value survives, with at most 3.6% relative error. Same 8 bits, completely different outcome.

blocks.md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

Computing amax needs a full pass over the tensor *before* casting it. Casting a BF16 tensor reads 2 bytes and writes 1 byte per element; a separate amax pass reads the 2 bytes again, so the scaling step moves about 5/3 as much memory as the cast alone. NVIDIA's Transformer Engine (TE), a library of FP8-aware PyTorch layers that does the casting and keeps the scales, offers two per-tensor strategies:

- **Delayed scaling** (`DelayedScaling`): use a scale derived from amaxes seen in *previous* iterations. Defaults: `amax_history_len=1024`, `amax_compute_algo='max'`, `margin=0`, `fp8_format=Format.HYBRID` (E4M3 in the forward pass, E5M2 for gradients in the backward pass). The new scale is `(FP8_MAX / amax) / 2^margin`.
- **Current scaling** (`Float8CurrentScaling`): compute amax from the tensor being cast right now.

Finer scales shrink this cost. A 1x128 tile's amax can be found while its 128 values are already loaded for the cast, which is how DeepSeek-V3 computes its scales *online*, with no history (lesson 3). DeepSeek still counts the remaining round trip as a cost: BF16 values are read from GPU memory, FP8 values written back, then read again by the GEMM, and the report asks future hardware to cast during the memory transfer itself.

blocks.title: Delayed scaling with a 4-step history (simplified)
blocks.code:
FP8_MAX = 448.0                 # E4M3
history = []                    # TE default keeps 1024 steps
scale = FP8_MAX / 3.0           # from an earlier step

for step, amax in enumerate(amaxes):
    used = scale                # chosen before seeing this step
    x_fp8 = cast_e4m3(x * used) # |x * used| > 448 saturates
    history = (history + [amax])[-4:]
    scale = FP8_MAX / max(history)   # amax_compute_algo = 'max'

scenes.caption: Step 0: amax 3.0 times scale 149.33 lands exactly on 448. The tensor uses the full E4M3 range.
Step 1: amax 2.8 maps to 418, safely inside the range. The history now holds two amaxes.
Step 3: still steady. The scale has not changed because the history max is still 3.0.
Step 4: a spike. amax 9.6 times the old scale is 1,434, far above 448. The values saturate: 9.6 is stored as 448, which decodes to 3.0. Only the next step's scale reacts.
Step 5: the history max is now 9.6, so the scale drops to 46.67 and amax 3.0 maps to only 140. No overflow, but the tensor sits about 1.7 binades below the top of the range.
Step 8: still the small scale. The spike leaves the 4-step window only after this step; with TE's default 1024-step history and 'max', it would linger for 1024 steps.

blocks.prompt: In the trace, the history window is 4 steps. TE's default window is 1024 steps with the 'max' rule. After a one-step amax spike of 3x, what happens to every later step's precision in TE's default setting?
blocks.reveal: For the next 1024 steps the scale stays about 3x smaller than needed, so each tensor uses only about the bottom $448/3 \approx 150$ of E4M3's range. Values keep their 3-bit relative precision in the normal range, but the smallest ones fall into the subnormal zone or to zero sooner. A long 'max' history is a safety choice: it rarely overflows, but one spike costs headroom for a long time.

blocks.md: Do not copy FP16's overflow handling. FP16 automatic mixed precision (PyTorch's autocast with a dynamic loss scaler) skips the update and shrinks the loss scale when an overflow appears. The FP8 paper explains that overflows are much more likely in FP8's narrow range, so skipping would discard too many steps; FP8 recipes **saturate** out-of-range values to the maximum instead.

blocks.code:
import torch
import transformer_engine.pytorch as te
from transformer_engine.common import recipe

layer = te.Linear(4096, 4096, bias=False, params_dtype=torch.bfloat16).cuda()
x = torch.randn(8192, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

fp8 = recipe.DelayedScaling(fp8_format=recipe.Format.HYBRID,
                            amax_history_len=1024, amax_compute_algo="max")
with te.autocast(enabled=True, recipe=fp8):
    y = layer(x)          # Fprop GEMM runs in FP8 (E4M3 inputs)
y.float().sum().backward()  # Dgrad and Wgrad GEMMs use E5M2 gradients
blocks.caption: Transformer Engine runs the GEMMs inside the autocast region in FP8 and manages amax histories and scales itself. Older code uses the deprecated name te.fp8_autocast(fp8_recipe=...).

blocks.question: With delayed scaling, the scale for step t comes from amaxes recorded up to step t-1. A layer's activations suddenly grow 4x at step t. What happens at step t?
options: Training stops with a NaN because E4M3 has no infinity
The largest values exceed 448 after scaling and saturate to 448, so they are clipped for that step
TE detects the overflow and skips the optimizer step
Nothing: the scale is recomputed from step t before casting
blocks.explain: Delayed scaling reacts one step late. At step t the old scale pushes the large values past 448 and they saturate (clip). The new amax enters the history, so step t+1 uses a smaller scale. Current scaling avoids this lag at the cost of an extra pass over the tensor.

blocks.question: Why multiply by $s$ *before* casting rather than cast first and multiply afterwards?
options: Multiplying after the cast is slower on tensor cores
Values lost to underflow or rounding during the cast cannot be recovered by multiplying later
The cast only accepts values between 0 and 1
It makes no difference; scaling commutes with rounding
blocks.explain: The cast is where information is destroyed: anything below the smallest representable value becomes 0 and everything else snaps to the grid. Scaling first moves the tensor to where the grid is dense enough. Scaling a zero afterwards still gives zero.

lessons.title: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion

blocks.md: Per-tensor scaling has a weak spot: one **outlier** sets the amax for millions of values. DeepSeek-V3 names outliers in activations, weights and gradients as the main obstacle to low-precision training: a few values far larger than the rest. With a per-tensor scale, everything else is squeezed toward the bottom of the range. In E4M3 a value more than $448 / 2^{-6} = 28{,}672$ times smaller than the amax falls into the subnormal zone, where relative precision collapses.

The DeepSeek-V3 report (671B-parameter MoE model trained in FP8: each feed-forward layer is split into many expert networks, and a small gating network sends each token to only a few of them) fixes this with **fine-grained scaling**:

- **Activations**: one scale per **1x128 tile**, that is per token per 128 channels (hidden features).
- **Weights**: one scale per **128x128 block** (128 input channels by 128 output channels).

Scales are computed **online** from the current tile's amax (no delayed history). Because each small group gets its own scale, DeepSeek uses E4M3 for *all* tensors, including gradients, instead of the E4M3/E5M2 hybrid.

blocks.title: Relative error (%) after E4M3: one scale vs one scale per row

scenes.caption: Simplified: 4 tokens x 8 channels stand in for 128-channel tiles. Token 2 has one value of 2000. With one per-tensor scale (448/2000), tokens 0 and 3 land in the subnormal zone: errors up to 16.3%.
With one scale per token row (a 1x8 tile here, 1x128 in DeepSeek-V3), each row uses the full range. Tokens 0 and 3 drop to at most 3.2% error; the outlier row is unchanged.
Max error per row, per-tensor vs per-tile: token 0: 12.8% vs 2.1%; token 3: 16.3% vs 3.2%. The outlier only hurts its own tile.

blocks.md: A linear layer runs three GEMMs: **Fprop** (forward propagation, $y = xW$), **Dgrad** (data gradient: the activation gradient $\partial x = \partial y \, W^T$, passed to earlier layers) and **Wgrad** (weight gradient: $\partial W = x^T \partial y$). The dimension a GEMM sums over is called **K**, its inner or reduction dimension: input channels for Fprop, output channels for Dgrad and tokens for Wgrad. DeepSeek-V3 runs all three in FP8 with outputs in BF16 or FP32. Because Wgrad consumes FP8 activations, the activations saved for the backward pass can be cached in FP8 too, which cuts memory.

blocks.title: One FP8 linear layer in DeepSeek-V3 (simplified)

scenes.caption: Forward: the BF16 activation is quantized per 1x128 tile and the FP32 master weight per 128x128 block. The Fprop GEMM consumes FP8 and writes BF16.
Backward, Dgrad: the incoming gradient dy is quantized to FP8 tiles and multiplied by the same FP8 weight blocks to produce dx for the previous layer.

Backward, Wgrad: the cached FP8 activation, re-tiled from 1x128 to 128x1 because K is now the token axis, meets dy. The weight gradient is kept in FP32 and AdamW (moments in BF16) updates the FP32 master weight.

blocks.md:
DeepSeek-V3 keeps several parts in their original precision (BF16 or FP32): the embedding, the output head, MoE gating, normalizations and attention. Master weights and weight gradients stay in FP32. To save memory it stores the AdamW moments (its running averages of the gradient and of the squared gradient) in BF16 and caches most activations in FP8.

One more problem is in the hardware. The report measured that FP8 GEMMs on H800 tensor cores (the H800 is a Hopper-generation GPU, the export version of the H100) accumulate, that is keep the running sum of products, with only about **14 bits** of precision. For two random matrices with K = 4096 this gave a maximum relative error of nearly 2%.

Why does 14-bit accumulation hurt? The accumulator is itself a float: keeping 14 significant bits, the gap between neighbouring values near a running sum $S$ is about $S / 2^{13}$. So the bigger the sum, the coarser the grid each new product is added onto.

A simplified model, computed with a script (simplified: DeepSeek's report says Hopper's tensor cores shift each product to the largest exponent and truncate beyond 14 bits, which is cruder than rounding): add 4,096 positive products, each between 1.0 and 1.2, into a 14-bit accumulator with round-to-nearest. Below a sum of 256 the gap is at most 1/64 and products land almost intact. Above 2,048 the gap is 0.25, so a product of 1.1 lands as 1.0 and one of 1.15 as 1.25. Above 4,096 the gap is 0.5 and *every* product between 1.0 and 1.2 is added as exactly 1.0: about 0.1 is lost on each add, always in the same direction.

blocks.title: Relative error of a 14-bit running sum (simplified model)

scenes.caption: One 14-bit accumulator for the whole sum. The error grows with K: about 0.01% at 128 products, 0.32% at 2,048 and 1.17% at 4,096 (mean of 40 random draws), the same order as the nearly 2% DeepSeek measured on H800.

Promotion: the 14-bit accumulator only ever sums 128 products (a partial sum near 140, gap 1/64), then each partial sum is added in FP32. The error at K = 4,096 falls to about 0.003%, some 400 times smaller.

blocks.md:
The fix is **promotion to CUDA cores**, in three parts:

- The tensor cores accumulate a partial sum over only $N_C = 128$ elements of K. On Hopper that is 4 WGMMA instructions (warpgroup-level matrix multiply-accumulate; a warpgroup is 4 warps), each covering 32 elements of K for FP8 inputs.
- The partial sum is copied to FP32 registers on the CUDA cores (the GPU's general-purpose units that run ordinary FP32 instructions) and added to a full-precision total. The per-tile scales sit along K, so they are multiplied in at the same moment, almost for free.
- While one warpgroup promotes, another keeps issuing MMAs, so the tensor cores stay busy.

blocks.title: Promoting partial sums to FP32 every 128 elements (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Default: one warpgroup accumulates all of K = 512 inside the tensor core at about 14-bit precision. Rounding error builds up as K grows.
DeepSeek-V3: after every 128 elements (4 WGMMAs) the partial sum is promoted and added in FP32, scales applied. Each tensor-core span only ever sums 128 products.

A second warpgroup fills the gaps: while A promotes, B issues its own MMAs, so the tensor cores rarely sit idle. The report finds 128 is the smallest interval that helps precision without large overhead.

blocks.md: With these changes, DeepSeek validated FP8 against BF16 on two MoE models (about 16B parameters on 1.33T tokens and about 230B on about 0.9T tokens): the relative loss error stayed below **0.25%**, within run-to-run noise.

Not every tensor tolerates coarse grouping. DeepSeek tried quantizing activation gradients in 128x128 blocks (so only a transpose would be needed in the backward pass). A 16B MoE model trained for about 300B tokens diverged: Dgrad feeds every earlier layer in a chain and is very precision-sensitive. Activation gradients keep fine 1x128 tiles.

Some FP8 failures only show up late. Fishman et al. (2024) trained FP8 LLMs on up to 2T tokens and found instabilities that shorter runs never revealed, caused by SwiGLU (the gated feed-forward activation of Llama-style models: a Swish-activated projection of the input times a second projection, so large inputs grow roughly quadratically) amplifying outliers over long training. Test recipes over long token horizons; lesson 6 explains the mechanism.

blocks.question: Why does DeepSeek-V3 scale activations per 1x128 tile instead of per tensor?
options: A single outlier would set the scale for the whole tensor and push ordinary values toward FP8's subnormal range; small tiles confine each outlier to its own 128 values
Tensor cores cannot read a per-tensor scale
Tiles let the model skip the Wgrad GEMM
Per-tile scales make the format exact, so no rounding happens
blocks.explain: Fine-grained scaling limits each outlier's damage to its own tile, so every other tile can use E4M3's full range. That is also what lets DeepSeek use E4M3 everywhere instead of E5M2 for gradients.

blocks.question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scales are stale; switch to delayed scaling
Too few mantissa bits in the inputs; switch all inputs to E5M2
Limited-precision accumulation inside the tensor cores; promote partial sums to FP32 every N_C elements
The output is BF16; write it in FP8 instead
blocks.explain: The DeepSeek report traces large-K error to about 14-bit accumulation in Hopper FP8 tensor cores and fixes it by moving partial sums to FP32 on CUDA cores every 128 elements. E5M2 inputs would make precision worse, not better.

lessons.title: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed

blocks.md:
Start with a measurement. The float8 training docs of torchao (PyTorch's library for quantized and low-precision training) report Llama3-8B on 8 H100 GPUs: in BF16 it ran 6,150 tokens per second at 47.65 GB peak memory; with FP8 GEMMs (per-tensor scaling) and FP8 weight all-gathers (the step, explained below, that collects each layer's sharded weights onto every GPU) it ran 7,689.5 tokens per second, a **25%** gain, at 47.77 GB. The GEMMs can run up to 2x faster, yet the step got only 1.25x faster and memory did not drop at all.

This lesson explains both numbers: where the rest of the time goes, where the memory actually lives, and how FP8-LM, DeepSeek-V3 and PyTorch's FSDP2 push FP8 into gradients, optimizer state and communication.

**Time.** Suppose a fraction $f$ of each training step is GEMMs and they run $r$ times faster. Everything else (attention softmax, normalizations, element-wise ops, communication that is not hidden) keeps its time, so the step speeds up by the formula below. This is *Amdahl's law*: the part you do not speed up limits the total.

Example, with an assumed $f = 0.7$ and $r = 2$: $1 / (0.3 + 0.35) = 1.54$x. Casting adds time too: torchao states that FP8 wins only when the BF16 GEMM time exceeds the FP8 GEMM time *plus* the amax and casting overhead, which holds for large matrices and fails for small ones, where FP8 can be slower than BF16.

blocks.caption: f is the fraction of step time spent in GEMMs before the change, r the GEMM speedup. Even with r very large the step speedup cannot exceed 1/(1 - f).

blocks.title: Step speedup when only the GEMMs get faster

x.label: fraction of step time in GEMMs (f)

scenes.caption: FP8 versus BF16 (r = 2). With GEMMs at 70% of the step, the step gets 1.54x faster, not 2x. Drag r to try other formats.
r = 4, the FP4 rate NVIDIA lists for GB200. At f = 0.7 the step speedup is only 2.1x: the other 30% now dominates.
r = 6 (FP4 on GB300) gives 2.4x at f = 0.7. Past a point, faster GEMMs buy little; shrinking the non-GEMM time matters more.

blocks.md: Published measurements, all on H100 GPUs. IBM and Meta's FSDP2 float8 blog reports throughput gains over BF16 of 18% at 1.8B parameters, 28% at 8B, 50% at 70B and 52% at 405B, with per-tensor scaling. Bigger models have bigger matrices, so both $f$ and the realized $r$ grow. FP8-LM measured GPT-175B at +21% with the same batch size, and +75% when the memory FP8 saved let them raise the micro-batch from 1 to 4.

blocks.title: Measured end-to-end throughput gain of FP8 over BF16

scenes.caption: Same recipe, growing model: the gain rises from 18% to about 50% as the GEMMs grow. None reach the 100% a 2x GEMM speedup suggests.
FP8-LM's 75% comes from using saved memory for a 4x larger micro-batch, not from faster arithmetic alone. Same batch: 21%.

blocks.md:
**Memory.** With the Adam optimizer, FP8-LM counts 16 bytes per parameter in standard mixed precision: an FP32 master weight (4), an FP32 gradient (4) and two FP32 Adam moments (4 + 4), the running averages of the gradient and of its square. FP8 GEMM inputs touch none of these, which is why the 8B run above saved no memory. DeepSeek-V3 keeps FP32 master weights and gradients but stores the moments in BF16: 12 bytes.

FP8-LM goes down to **6 bytes**: master weight in FP16 with a scale factor (2), gradient in FP8 (1), first moment in FP8 (1), second moment in FP16 (2). The first moment tolerates FP8 because Adam relies mostly on the gradient's direction. The second moment squares small gradients, which underflow, and Adam divides by its square root, so its smallest values matter most. Fishman et al. later stored both moments in FP8, with E5M2's extra range for the second.

blocks.title: Weights, gradients and Adam state per parameter

scenes.caption: Bytes per parameter for master weight, gradient and both Adam moments. Activations are extra and depend on batch and sequence length.
For a 7B-parameter model: 112 GB, 84 GB and 42 GB. FP8-LM measured 39% less real memory than BF16 for GPT-175B.

blocks.md:
**Communication.** In data-parallel training each GPU (a *rank*) computes gradients on its own batch, and an **all-reduce** sums them across all N ranks so every rank gets the total. Sending FP8 halves the bytes of BF16, but FP8-LM found two problems.

First, range. *Pre-scaling* (divide each gradient by N, then sum) pushes small values into underflow when N is large; *post-scaling* (sum, then divide) can overflow during the sum. FP8-LM's *automatic scaling* multiplies gradients by a factor $\mu$: if more than 0.001% of values sit at the FP8 maximum, $\mu$ is halved for the next step; otherwise it grows exponentially to 2 over 1,000 steps.

Second, the scales. Each rank's FP8 gradient carries its own per-tensor scale, but NCCL (NVIDIA's collective communication library) adds raw elements and cannot apply a different scale per rank. FP8-LM first all-reduces one scalar, the minimum scale over ranks, and every rank requantizes with it. The minimum is safe: it makes every rank's values smallest, so none overflows.

blocks.title: All-reducing FP8 gradients with a shared scale

scenes.caption: Both ranks hold the gradient value 0.003 for the same weight. Rank 0 uses scale 1000 and stores 3; rank 1's tensor had a smaller amax, so its scale is 4000 and it stores 12.
Summing raw FP8 values gives 15. Decoded with scale 1000 that is 0.015, with 4000 it is 0.00375. The true sum is 0.006: neither scale is right.
FP8-LM first all-reduces the scales and keeps the minimum, 1000. Rank 1 requantizes: 0.003 x 1000 = 3.
Now a standard all-reduce of FP8 values gives 6, with scale N x 1000 = 2000. Decoding gives 0.003, which is the mean gradient: dividing by N is folded into the scale.

blocks.md:
Other collectives follow the same pattern:

- **MoE all-to-all.** DeepSeek-V3 quantizes activations to FP8 before the *dispatch* (the all-to-all that sends each token to the GPUs holding its experts), with power-of-two scales, and does the same for the activation gradient before the down-projections. It keeps the *combine* (gathering expert outputs back) in BF16.
- **Tensor and sequence parallelism** (splitting each layer's weight matrices, or its tokens, across GPUs). FP8-LM sends FP8 activations through the all-gather and reduce-scatter between these regions, cutting activation communication by 34%. Separately, FP8 weights and gradients cut its weight-related communication for GPT-7B by 63%.
- **FSDP2.** In fully sharded data parallelism each rank stores a slice of every weight and all-gathers the full weight just before using it. PyTorch's FSDP2 can do that all-gather in float8; the IBM and Meta blog measured about 5% extra throughput from it, beyond FP8 compute.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torchao.float8 import Float8LinearConfig, convert_to_float8_training

m = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8192, 4096, bias=False),
                  nn.Linear(4096, 128, bias=False)).bfloat16().cuda()

def module_filter_fn(mod, fqn):
    if fqn == "1":                  # keep the last layer in BF16
        return False
    if isinstance(mod, nn.Linear):  # FP8 GEMMs need dims divisible by 16
        return mod.in_features % 16 == 0 and mod.out_features % 16 == 0
    return True

# recipes: "tensorwise" (fastest), "rowwise", "rowwise_with_gw_hp" (most accurate)
config = Float8LinearConfig.from_recipe_name("tensorwise")
convert_to_float8_training(m, config=config, module_filter_fn=module_filter_fn)
m = torch.compile(m)                # needed for competitive speed
blocks.caption: Adapted from torchao's float8 training quick start. Not run here: it needs an H100-class GPU. Only nn.Linear layers become FP8; FSDP2's float8 all-gather is configured in the distributed setup (torchtitan has end-to-end examples).

blocks.md: A 2x faster GEMM is not a 2x faster step: the speedup is capped by the non-GEMM share of time and eaten into by casting overhead. FP8 GEMM inputs also save almost no memory; the bytes live in master weights, gradients and optimizer state, and in communication, which need their own FP8 treatment (shared scales, automatic scaling).

blocks.question: Two data-parallel ranks quantize their gradients to FP8 with their own per-tensor scales and run a standard all-reduce on the raw FP8 values. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because all-reduce is a sum and sums commute
The all-reduce overflows on every step
NCCL rejects FP8 tensors
The summed values mix two different scales, so no single scale decodes the sum correctly
blocks.explain: Each stored value means value divided by its own rank's scale. Adding 3 (scale 1000) and 12 (scale 4000) gives 15, which decodes to neither 0.006 nor anything meaningful. FP8-LM all-reduces the minimum scale first, requantizes, and only then sums.

blocks.question: GEMMs take 60% of a BF16 training step. FP4 makes them 4x faster and nothing else changes. What is the best possible step speedup?
options: About 1.8x
4x
blocks.explain: 1 / ((1 - 0.6) + 0.6 / 4) = 1 / (0.4 + 0.15) = 1.82. The 40% that is not GEMM work now dominates the step. Casting overhead would lower it further.

blocks.question: A team turns on FP8 GEMMs for every linear layer and expects peak memory to halve. It barely changes. Why?
options: FP8 tensors are padded to 16 bits in memory
Most memory is master weights, gradients, optimizer moments and activations that FP8 GEMM inputs do not touch
The amax history uses more memory than the weights
Tensor cores cannot read FP8 from memory
blocks.explain: FP8 GEMMs change compute, not the 12 to 16 bytes per parameter of training state. FP8-LM cut memory by moving the gradient and first moment to FP8 and the master weight and second moment to FP16, and DeepSeek-V3 caches activations in FP8.

lessons.title: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values

blocks.md: DeepSeek-V3 had to multiply its 1x128 scales in software on CUDA cores. **Microscaling (MX)** puts fine-grained scales into the format, so the tensor core applies them itself. The Open Compute Project (OCP, an industry group that publishes open hardware specifications) MX specification, described by Rouhani et al. (2023), defines a **block** of $k = 32$ elements that share one 8-bit scale $X$ stored as **E8M0**: an 8-bit exponent with no mantissa (bias 127), so $X$ is always a power of two between $2^{-127}$ and $2^{127}$.

The concrete formats differ only in the element type:

- **MXFP8**: E4M3 or E5M2 elements
- **MXFP6**: E2M3 or E3M2 elements
- **MXFP4**: E2M1 elements
- **MXINT8**: 8-bit integer elements

Each element decodes as $v_i = X \cdot P_i$, where $P_i$ is the stored element; lowercase $v_i$ is the decoded value and capital $V_i$ the original value it approximates. The reference conversion (Algorithm 1 in the paper) picks the shared exponent from the block's amax, then rounds each $V_i / X$ to the element format, clamping anything above its maximum. In words: $X$ is 2 to the power (floor of $\log_2$ amax, minus $e_{\max}$), where $e_{\max}$ is the exponent of the element format's largest normal number. The floor finds the amax's power of two, and subtracting $e_{\max}$ moves that power onto the element format's top binade, so the scaled amax lands in the top binade and can even pass the element maximum, which is why clamping is needed.

blocks.caption: 6 = 1.5 x 2^2, so e_max is 2 for E2M1; 448 = 1.75 x 2^8, so e_max is 8 for E4M3.

blocks.title: One MXFP4 block of 32 values

scenes.caption: A block of 32 values: most are between 0.02 and 0.6, and one outlier is 3.2 (index 19). One E8M0 scale must serve all 32.
OCP rule: floor(log2 3.2) = 1, minus e_max 2, gives X = 2^-1 = 0.5. Now 3.2 / 0.5 = 6.4 exceeds FP4's 6 and is clamped: 3.2 decodes as 3.0. Values under 0.125 become 0 (11 zeros in total).

Round-up rule (MXFP8 recipe of Mishra et al.): X = 2^ceil(log2(3.2/6)) = 1, so nothing clamps. But 3.2 still rounds to 3, the FP4 codes 4 and 6 go unused, and values up to 0.25 vanish (0.25 is a tie and rounds to even, 0): 19 zeros.
The root cause is the power-of-two scale: the block's amax can never be mapped exactly onto 6. Either it overflows and clamps (round down) or a binade of FP4 codes is wasted (round up).

blocks.prompt: Under the round-up rule, a block's amax is $3 + \delta$ for a tiny $\delta$. Which FP4 magnitudes can that block never use, and how much of FP4's range is lost?
blocks.reveal: The ideal decode scale is $(3+\delta)/6 = 0.5 + \delta/6$, which rounds up to the power of two 1. The scaled amax is $3 + \delta$, which rounds to 3, so **4 and 6 are never used**. The NVFP4 paper computes the damage: the block spans only $\log_2(3/0.5) = 2.58$ binades instead of $\log_2(6/0.5) = 3.58$, losing nearly one binade.

blocks.md: For 8-bit elements the waste matters much less, and MXFP8 is already a production format. Mishra et al. (2025) report that two choices make MXFP8 pretraining match BF16 (models up to 8B parameters, up to 15T tokens): use **E4M3 for all tensors**, including activation gradients, and **round the scale up** rather than down as the OCP v1.0 reference suggests, so no scaled value overflows.

blocks.prompt: Take Gaussian blocks of 32 values and the OCP round-down rule. For MXFP8 with E4M3 elements the scaled amax lands in [256, 512) but E4M3 stops at 448. What fraction of blocks clamp their largest value? And for MXFP4, whose top binade is [4, 8) with maximum 6?
blocks.reveal:
A block clamps when its amax divided by its power of two exceeds 448 / 256 = **1.75** (E4M3) or 6 / 4 = **1.5** (E2M1). In a simulation of 100,000 Gaussian blocks (computed with a script), **16.9%** of MXFP8 blocks clamped their amax, cutting it by 7% on average and up to 12.5%. For MXFP4, **29.5%** of blocks clamped, by up to 25%.

The largest value of a block is exactly the one most likely to matter. Rounding the scale up makes the count zero, which Mishra et al. adopted after OCP-rule MXFP8 runs showed training issues they hypothesize come from these overflows.

blocks.md:
Why E4M3 even for gradients? Per-tensor FP8 used E5M2 for gradients because one scale had to cover the whole tensor's spread. With one scale per 32 values, a block only needs the spread *inside* it: in the same Gaussian simulation, about 6 values in a million sit more than 17.8 binades (E4M3's whole range) below their block's amax. Mishra et al. say the same: at 32-element blocks, E4M3's 17.8 binades cover the range, and then precision matters.

The figure uses a simplified gradient-like tensor (computed with a script): 4,096 rows of 32 Gaussian values, each row multiplied by $2^u$ with $u$ uniform in [-24, 0], so rows span 24 binades.

blocks.title: A tensor whose rows span 24 binades, four ways

scenes.caption: Values flushed to 0. One E4M3 scale loses a third of the tensor; E5M2's 32 binades or a scale per block lose nothing.
Median relative error of the values. Once blocks supply the range, E4M3's extra mantissa bit halves the error (2.2% versus 4.3%). Mishra et al. found an 8B model needed E4M3 gradients.

blocks.md:
Two practical costs:

- **Storage**: one 8-bit scale per 32 elements adds $8/32 = 0.25$ bits per element, so MXFP8 costs 8.25 bits and MXFP4 4.25 bits per value. For 12B weights: 24.0 GB in BF16, 12.375 GB in MXFP8, 6.375 GB in MXFP4.
- **Transposes**: a block runs along one axis, usually the GEMM's reduction dimension. The backward pass needs $W^T$, whose blocks run the other way, and quantizing then transposing is not the same as transposing then quantizing. Both versions must be made from the high-precision tensor.

MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

blocks.question: A training framework quantizes W to MXFP8 row-wise for Fprop, then reuses the same quantized tensor, transposed, for Dgrad. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because transposing does not change values
MXFP8 cannot be transposed in memory
The E8M0 scales overflow after transposing
The transposed tensor's blocks now run along the wrong axis; the backward pass must quantize W along the other axis from the high-precision copy
blocks.explain: MX scales are shared along one axis. Dgrad reduces over the other dimension of W, so it needs blocks along that axis. The MX paper and Transformer Engine both produce the transposed version directly from the high-precision tensor to avoid double quantization error.

blocks.question: In the round-up example above (X = 1), which input magnitudes decode to exactly 0?
options: Below 0.25
Below 0.5
Below 0.125
None: FP4 has no zero
blocks.explain: With X = 1 the smallest positive FP4 value is 0.5, and round-to-nearest sends anything below the midpoint 0.25 to 0. In the 32-value block that wiped out 19 of 32 values, more than half.

lessons.title: When low precision fails: outliers, SwiGLU and debugging a run

blocks.md:
Picture one hidden state of a transformer layer: thousands of numbers, the median about 0.2 in magnitude, and one value of 2,000. That is not a thought experiment. Sun et al. (2024) found such **massive activations** in many LLMs: in LLaMA2-7B, values around 10,000 times the median magnitude, and in LLaMA2-70B values above 15,000. They are rare (often fewer than 10 among tens of millions of activations) and sit in the *residual stream*, the running sum $h_\ell = h_{\ell-1} + F_\ell(h_{\ell-1})$ that each layer adds its output to.

Lesson 3 called outliers the main obstacle to low precision. This lesson shows where they come from, one mechanism that grows them late in training, and how to debug a run that fails.

blocks.title: Largest activation magnitudes in one LLaMA2-7B hidden state

scenes.caption: Magnitudes from Sun et al.'s Table 1: 2,622, 1,547 and 802 at the top, 0.2 at the median. On a linear axis everything but the top few is invisible.
The same values as binades above the median (log2 of value / 0.2): the top value is 13.7 binades up. E4M3 spans about 18 binades in total and an FP4 block only 3.58.

blocks.md:
Massive activations are not noise. They appear abruptly after one early layer (layer 2 in LLaMA2-7B), stay nearly constant through the middle layers and fade in the last few. They live in a few fixed feature dimensions (1415 and 2533 in LLaMA2-7B), on the starting token and delimiter tokens such as the first period or newline, and barely depend on the input. Setting four of them to zero collapses LLaMA2-7B, while setting them to their mean values does not hurt: they act as fixed **bias terms** the model learned to store in its hidden state, and they pull attention toward their tokens.

So a quantizer must keep them, not clip them, and must not let them wipe out their neighbours.

blocks.title: One token with a massive activation, quantized two ways

scenes.caption: Simplified: 8 channels of one token, with a massive activation of 2,000 in channel 3.
One E4M3 scale for these values (448 / 2000 = 0.224). E4M3's 18 binades cope: errors stay under 5% except -0.02, which lands in the subnormal zone (12.8% error).
An NVFP4 block containing the 2,000 (8 values standing in for 16): block scale 333, smallest nonzero step 167, so all seven ordinary values decode to 0.

blocks.md:
A second source of outliers grows during training. **SwiGLU**, the feed-forward activation of Llama-style models, computes for each neuron the product of two projections of the input $x$: $x^\top w_1$ times $\text{Swish}(x^\top w_2)$, where $\text{Swish}(z) = z\,\sigma(z)$ and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. Its output is the input of the layer's last linear map $w_3$.

ReLU, GeLU (Gaussian error linear unit, $x$ times the probability that a standard Gaussian is below $x$) and Swish grow at most linearly in their input. SwiGLU multiplies two projections, so when $w_1$ and $w_2$ point the same way it grows with the *square* of the input: Fishman et al. note that with $w_1 = w_2$ and $w_1^\top x = 1$, $\text{SwiGLU}(cx) / c^2$ tends to 1 as $c$ grows.

blocks.caption: From Fishman et al. (2024). Each factor is linear in x, so the product is quadratic when the two projections agree.

blocks.title: SwiGLU grows quadratically once its weights align

scenes.caption: Simplified model: x^T w1 = c and x^T w2 = rho c. With little alignment (rho = 0.1) SwiGLU stays moderate.
rho = 0.5: the output at c = 30 is about 450, roughly 15 times what Swish alone gives.
Fully aligned (rho = 1): output about c squared, 900 at c = 30. A modest input becomes an extreme value feeding w3.

blocks.md: Fishman et al. trained Llama2-architecture models in FP8 (E4M3 forward, E5M2 backward, delayed scaling) on up to 2T tokens. The FP8 run diverged after about 200B tokens, when sporadic outliers appeared that earlier training never showed. They prove that with $\ell_2$ regularization (weight decay), at a stationary point of training (where the gradient of the loss is zero), $w_1$ and $w_2$ of a SwiGLU neuron with large enough inputs converge to the same or opposite direction. In an outlier channel they measured exactly that: the correlation of $w_1$ and $w_2$ rose sharply between 125B and 210B tokens while the norm of $w_2$ grew. Turning off FP8 quantization of the SwiGLU output alone removed the divergence.

blocks.title: One SwiGLU neuron as its weights align (worked example)

scenes.caption: Input x = [2, 2, 2, 2]. u1 = x.w1 = 4, u2 = x.w2 = 1, output 4 x 1 x sigmoid(1) = 2.92. Delayed scaling expects amax 4 (scale 112): 2.92 is stored as 320 and decodes as 2.86.
Training rotates w2 toward w1 (correlation 0.5): u2 = 2, output 7.05. Scaled by 112 that is 789, past 448: it saturates and decodes as 4.0.
Fully aligned (w2 = w1): u2 = 4, output 15.71, scaled 1,760. Still stored as 448, still decoded as 4.0.
Aligned and both norms doubled: u1 = u2 = 8, output 63.98, about 4x the aligned value: both projections doubled. Clipped to 4.0, the value feeding w3 is off by 94%.
Smooth-SwiGLU: this channel gets its own scale from its own max (448 / 63.98), so 63.98 maps to 448 exactly and decodes intact. The scale is undone after w3.

blocks.md: **Smooth-SwiGLU** is Fishman et al.'s fix. Before the SwiGLU output is quantized, each channel $i$ is multiplied by its own scale $s_i$, computed from that channel's maximum (the tensor is split into per-channel chunks whose maxima are found in parallel); after the $w_3$ GEMM the scale is divided back out. The function is unchanged, only its quantization is. At inference the scales fold into the weights of $w_1$ and $w_3$. Combined with FP8 storage of both Adam moments, they trained a 7B model on 256 Intel Gaudi2 accelerators matching the BF16 baseline, with up to about 34% higher throughput.

blocks.tex: \text{Smooth-SwiGLU}_{\hat w_{1,i},\hat w_{2,i}}(x) = s_i^{-1}\cdot Q\!\left(s_i\cdot (\hat w_{1,i}^\top Q(x))\,\text{Swish}(\hat w_{2,i}^\top Q(x))\right)
blocks.caption: Q is the quantizer and a hat marks a quantized weight. The per-channel scale s_i is applied before Q and removed after, so only the rounding changes.

blocks.md:
Even without a single culprit, lower precision narrows the space of settings that train. Lee et al. (*To FP8 and Back Again*) emulate formats with fewer bits by masking mantissa bits and clamping exponents, and report:

- Removing even one exponent bit from BF16 (E7M7) stopped training altogether; mantissa bits degrade more gradually.
- With fewer mantissa bits (E8M3, E8M4) Llama models diverged early, and E8M5 showed more frequent loss spikes at a 10x higher learning rate.
- MS-AMP's FP8 (the FP8-LM code) matched BF16 on a clean dataset but on OpenWebText left a gap that 6x more steps did not close, larger when the output head was quantized too.

Their point: a low-precision recipe is only cheaper if it is as robust as BF16 across seeds, learning rates and data; restarts after a divergence can erase the speedup.

blocks.prompt: Lee et al. ran nanoGPT's (a tiny GPT trainer) default GPT-2 recipe in ordinary BF16 mixed precision for 5% of its training, with 188 different random seeds and nothing else changed. How many runs diverged? And with TF32 (NVIDIA's tensor-core float with BF16's range and three more mantissa bits)?
blocks.reveal:
**18 of 188** BF16 runs diverged, about 10%, and none of 70 TF32 runs did. Even the default 16-bit recipe fails on some seeds, and since only 5% of training was run the true rate is likely higher.

So a single successful low-precision run proves little. Compare *distributions* over seeds, and expect narrower formats to fail more often, not just converge slightly worse.

scenes.caption: Start from a gap you can trust: the same seed and the same data order in BF16 (the FSDP2 blog used a deterministic loader to replay data). DeepSeek-V3 accepted FP8 at under 0.25% relative loss error.

Log statistics per layer and per GEMM input: amax, the fraction flushed to zero and the fraction at the format max. FP8-LM compared its scaling strategies by SNR, underflow rate and overflow rate per Transformer block.
Find the first layer whose statistics drift, and which tensor (activation, weight or gradient). The NVFP4 report's analysis found larger Wgrad quantization error in the last layers.

Move that layer or tensor to higher precision and resume. If the gap closes, you have located the cause; fix it properly and re-test over a long horizon, since the SwiGLU failure needed about 200B tokens.

blocks.md: Do not trust a short run. Fishman et al.'s divergence appeared after about 200B tokens, twice the length of earlier FP8 studies, and Lee et al. expect their own short runs underestimate instability. A recipe that matches BF16 for a few billion tokens has only passed the easy part.

blocks.question: Why did Fishman et al.'s FP8 runs diverge only after roughly 200B tokens?
options: The learning rate warmup ended at 200B tokens
Weight decay slowly aligns the two SwiGLU weight vectors in some channels; once aligned, their output grows quadratically and saturates FP8
E4M3 accumulates rounding error linearly with tokens seen
The data mixture changed at that point
blocks.explain: Their theorem and measurements show w1 and w2 aligning in outlier channels (correlation rising sharply between 125B and 210B tokens) while norms grow. Delayed scaling cannot anticipate the sporadic spikes, and the SwiGLU output saturates.

blocks.question: Setting LLaMA2-7B's four massive activations to their mean values leaves the model working, while setting them to zero collapses it. What does that imply for quantization?
options: They are noise and can be clipped to the format maximum
They only matter at inference, not in training
They should be removed with weight decay
They are essential fixed biases: a quantizer must represent them, and must not let them flush their neighbours to zero
blocks.explain: Sun et al. conclude they work like constant bias terms. Clipping or zeroing them changes the model's function, and a shared scale sized for them can zero ordinary values: that is why per-block scaling, Smooth-SwiGLU style per-channel scales and higher-precision layers exist.

blocks.question: Your FP8 run matches BF16 for 50B tokens, then its loss slowly drifts above the baseline. Which step comes first?
options: Compare per-layer amax, underflow and saturation statistics against the BF16 run to find where they start to drift
Switch every layer to E5M2
Lower the learning rate by 10x and continue
Restart from scratch with a different seed
blocks.explain: Without locating the layer and tensor you cannot fix the cause. E5M2 everywhere trades precision for range blindly, a lower learning rate changes the experiment, and a new seed only hides the problem.

lessons.title: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale

blocks.md:
**NVFP4** is NVIDIA's 4-bit format for Blackwell. Its elements are the same E2M1 as MXFP4, but it changes the scaling in three ways:

1. **Blocks of 16** instead of 32, so each scale covers a narrower slice of the data.
2. Block scales stored in **E4M3** instead of E8M0, so a scale can be fractional (like 0.095) instead of a power of two.
3. A second, **per-tensor FP32 scale**, because E4M3 scales only reach up to 448 and down to $2^{-9}$: the tensor scale shifts the whole tensor so every block scale fits.

Two kinds of scale appear below. A **decode** scale turns a stored value back into a real one (real = stored x decode); an **encode** scale is its reciprocal, applied before rounding (stored = round(real x encode)). NVFP4 uses a per-tensor FP32 encode scale $s_{\text{enc}}$ and per-block decode scales $s_{\text{dec},b}$.

A block's decode scale is its amax over 6, which can be tiny: 0.0083 for a block whose amax is 0.05, inside E4M3's subnormal zone. So before it is rounded to E4M3 it is multiplied by $s_{\text{enc}}$, which lifts the largest block scale exactly to 448 and every other one below it. The FP32 tensor decode scale $1 / s_{\text{enc}}$ divides that factor back out after the GEMM.

blocks.caption: From Appendix B of the NVFP4 pretraining paper. 6 and 448 are the E2M1 and E4M3 maxima. The tensor core multiplies each 16-element partial dot product by both operands' block scales; the per-tensor scales are applied to the final output.

blocks.md:
In words: the tensor scale $s_{\text{enc}}$ is $6 \times 448 = 2688$ divided by the tensor amax. A block's ideal decode scale is its amax over 6, which puts the block amax on FP4's 6. Multiplying by $s_{\text{enc}}$ and rounding to E4M3 gives the stored block scale; the block holding the tensor amax lands exactly on 448, the top of E4M3, and every other block fits below. Each value is then divided by its effective scale, stored block scale over $s_{\text{enc}}$, and rounded to E2M1.

Run it on the same 32 values, treated as a tiny tensor of two 16-value blocks.

- Tensor amax is 3.2, so $s_{\text{enc}} = 2688 / 3.2 = 840$.
- **Block 1** amax is 0.58. Its ideal scale 0.0967 x 840 = 81.2 rounds to the E4M3 value **80**, so the effective scale is 80 / 840 = 0.0952.
- **Block 2** amax is 3.2. Its scale is 0.5333 x 840 = **448** exactly, so 3.2 maps exactly onto FP4's 6.

blocks.title: The same 32 values in NVFP4 (two blocks of 16)

scenes.caption: Start from the MXFP4 round-up result: one scale of 1.0 for all 32 values, 19 zeros, and the outlier decoded as 3.
Block 1 gets its own E4M3 scale of 0.0952. Its amax 0.58 maps to FP4's 6 and decodes as 0.571. Its smallest nonzero step is 0.5 x 0.0952 = 0.048, so none of its values become 0.
Block 2 still contains the outlier, so its scale is 0.533: 3.2 is stored exactly, but 6 small values in this block still round to 0. The outlier only hurts its own 16 values.

blocks.title: Quantization error on the 32-value example

scenes.caption: Mean squared error x 1000. NVFP4's finer blocks and fractional scales roughly halve the error of OCP-rule MXFP4 and cut round-up MXFP4's by more than 5x on this example.
Values decoded as exactly 0 out of 32. Fewer zeros means fewer small gradients or activations silently dropped.

blocks.md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

The price: 4 + 8/16 = **4.5 bits per element** versus 4.25 for MXFP4 (6.75 GB versus 6.375 GB for 12B weights), plus an extra pass over memory to find the tensor-wide amax before quantizing. The paper notes that the global scale could be computed over smaller regions to avoid that round trip. On Blackwell both FP4 formats run at the same tensor-core rate: 4x BF16 on GB200 and 6x on GB300.

blocks.question: Why does NVFP4 need a per-tensor FP32 scale while MXFP4 does not?
options: FP32 scales make the GEMM run faster
E4M3 block scales cover a much narrower range than E8M0 (at most 448 and at least 2^-9), so the tensor must first be shifted so all its block scales fit
Because NVFP4 elements are E4M3 instead of E2M1
To store the sign of each block
blocks.explain: E8M0 spans 2^-127 to 2^127, enough for any block scale. E4M3 trades that range for 3 mantissa bits. The FP32 tensor scale maps the largest block scale onto 448 so the rest fit underneath.

blocks.question: A tensor has amax 10. One block's amax is 0.05. What is that block's ideal scale before E4M3 rounding, in the stored (multiplied) form?
options: 448, like every block
blocks.explain: First s_enc = 6 x 448 / 10 = 268.8. The block's decode scale is 0.05 / 6 = 0.00833, and the stored value is 0.00833 x 268.8 = 2.24, comfortably inside E4M3's range. Without the tensor scale, 0.0083 would sit in E4M3's subnormal region.

lessons.title: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4

blocks.md:
Every number in this course so far was computed for you. Now build the tool that computed them: a **fake quantizer**. It rounds an ordinary float array onto a low-precision grid and immediately decodes it back, so the result is still a float array, but carrying exactly the rounding error the real format would add. Tiny example: fake-quantizing 0.3 to E2M1 gives 0.5, and 0.2 gives 0.

This is how recipes are prototyped before (or without) the hardware: Lee et al. emulated narrower formats by masking bits, Wang et al. emulated FP4 on H100 FP8 tensor cores, and Chmiel et al. simulated FP4 on Intel Gaudi2. Everything below runs on a laptop with NumPy, and all outputs shown are from real runs.

One rule covers every format. With $e$ exponent bits, $m$ mantissa bits and bias $2^{e-1}-1$, a magnitude $a$ lives in the binade with exponent $\lfloor \log_2 a \rfloor$, clamped below at $1 - \text{bias}$ (subnormals all share the lowest binade's step). Inside that binade neighbouring values are $2^{\text{exponent} - m}$ apart. So rounding is: divide by the step, round to the nearest integer with ties to even, multiply back, and saturate at the format maximum.

Check it against lesson 1: 300 in E4M3 has exponent 8 and step $2^{8-3} = 32$; 300 / 32 = 9.375 rounds to 9, giving 288.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

E4M3, E2M1 = (4, 3, 448.0), (2, 1, 6.0)  # (exp bits, mantissa bits, max)

def cast(x, e, m, vmax, rng=None):
    # Round onto the grid of an e-exponent, m-mantissa float format.
    bias = 2 ** (e - 1) - 1
    a = np.abs(x)
    ex = np.floor(np.log2(np.maximum(a, 1e-30)))
    ex = np.maximum(ex, 1 - bias)      # subnormals share the lowest step
    step = 2.0 ** (ex - m)             # gap between neighbours here
    if rng is None:
        q = np.round(a / step)         # numpy rounds ties to even
    else:                              # stochastic rounding
        lo = np.floor(a / step)
        q = lo + (rng.random(a.shape) < a / step - lo)
    return np.sign(x) * np.minimum(q * step, vmax)  # saturate
blocks.caption: Part 1 of the fake quantizer. A format is (exponent bits, mantissa bits, max). numpy's round sends ties to the even neighbour, which is the last-mantissa-bit-0 rule of lesson 1.

blocks.title: Tracing cast() on four values
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

E4M3, E2M1 = (4, 3, 448.0), (2, 1, 6.0)  # (exp bits, mantissa bits, max)

def cast(x, e, m, vmax, rng=None):
    # Round onto the grid of an e-exponent, m-mantissa float format.
    bias = 2 ** (e - 1) - 1
    a = np.abs(x)
    ex = np.floor(np.log2(np.maximum(a, 1e-30)))
    ex = np.maximum(ex, 1 - bias)      # subnormals share the lowest step
    step = 2.0 ** (ex - m)             # gap between neighbours here
    if rng is None:
        q = np.round(a / step)         # numpy rounds ties to even
    else:                              # stochastic rounding
        lo = np.floor(a / step)
        q = lo + (rng.random(a.shape) < a / step - lo)
    return np.sign(x) * np.minimum(q * step, vmax)  # saturate

scenes.caption: 300 in E4M3: exponent 8, step 32, 300 / 32 = 9.375 rounds to 9, so 288 (lesson 1's predict).
0.2 in E2M1: log2 gives -3, clamped to 0 (the subnormal exponent for bias 1), so the step is 0.5. 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4 rounds to 0: underflow.
1.25 in E2M1 is a tie between 1.0 and 1.5: 1.25 / 0.5 = 2.5, and ties go to the even integer 2, so 1.0.
500 in E4M3: step 32, 500 / 32 = 15.625 rounds to 16, which is 512, then saturates to the max 448.
With an rng the same value is rounded stochastically: 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4, so it becomes 0.5 with probability 0.4 and 0 otherwise.

blocks.md:
Part 2 adds the three scaling schemes on top of `cast`:

- `per_tensor`: one scale that maps the tensor's amax onto the format max (lesson 2).
- `mx`: one power-of-two scale per 32 values, either the OCP rule $2^{\lfloor \log_2 \text{amax} \rfloor - e_{\max}}$ or Mishra et al.'s round-up rule (lesson 5).
- `nvfp4`: an FP32 tensor encode scale, E4M3 block scales per 16 values, and E2M1 elements (lesson 7). Passing an `rng` turns on stochastic rounding.

blocks.code:
def per_tensor(x, fmt=E4M3):
    s = fmt[2] / np.abs(x).max()
    return cast(x * s, *fmt) / s

def mx(x, fmt=E2M1, emax=2, k=32, up=False):
    b = x.reshape(-1, k)
    amax = np.abs(b).max(1, keepdims=True)
    if up:   # round the scale up: nothing overflows
        X = 2.0 ** np.ceil(np.log2(amax / fmt[2]))
    else:    # OCP v1.0 reference: floor(log2 amax) - emax
        X = 2.0 ** (np.floor(np.log2(amax)) - emax)
    return (cast(b / X, *fmt) * X).reshape(x.shape)

def nvfp4(x, k=16, rng=None):
    s_enc = 6 * 448 / np.abs(x).max()          # FP32 tensor scale
    b = x.reshape(-1, k)
    amax_b = np.abs(b).max(1, keepdims=True)
    s_b = cast(amax_b / 6 * s_enc, *E4M3)      # stored E4M3 block scale
    eff = s_b / s_enc                           # effective decode scale
    return (cast(b / eff, *E2M1, rng) * eff).reshape(x.shape)
blocks.caption: Part 2. Blocks run along the last axis, so x.reshape(-1, k) puts one block per row. The scales stay in float64, exactly as the formats' FP32 or E8M0 scales would decode.

First test: the 32-value block of lessons 5 and 7. If the quantizer is right it must reproduce the figures there exactly.

```
MXFP4 down MSE x1000   6.54  zeros 11
MXFP4 up   MSE x1000  19.74  zeros 19
NVFP4      MSE x1000   3.47  zeros 6
```

It does: mean squared error x 1000 of 6.54, 19.74 and 3.47, and 11, 19 and 6 values flushed to zero.

blocks.md: Second test: a stress tensor. 4,096 standard Gaussian values with 4 values replaced by 50, outliers at 50 standard deviations. For the ordinary values we report the **signal-to-quantization-noise ratio** (SQNR): $10 \log_{10}$ of the signal power over the error power, in decibels. Every 6 dB means the error's amplitude halved ($10 \log_{10} 4 = 6.02$). We also report the fraction of ordinary values flushed to zero.

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.standard_normal(4096)
x[rng.choice(4096, 4, replace=False)] = 50.0   # 4 outliers at 50 sigma
norm = np.abs(x) < 50                          # the ordinary values

def report(name, q):
    err = x - q
    sqnr = 10 * np.log10(np.sum(x[norm]**2) / np.sum(err[norm]**2))
    print(f"{name:12s} MSE {np.mean(err**2):.5f}  SQNR {sqnr:5.1f} dB"
          f"  zeros {np.mean(q[norm] == 0):6.1%}")

report("E4M3 tensor", per_tensor(x))
report("E2M1 tensor", per_tensor(x, E2M1))
report("MXFP4 down", mx(x))
report("MXFP4 up", mx(x, up=True))
report("NVFP4", nvfp4(x))
report("NVFP4 SR", nvfp4(x, rng=rng))
blocks.caption: Part 4: six schemes on one outlier-heavy tensor. Seed 0, so the run is reproducible.

blocks.prompt: Before looking: which scheme flushes the most ordinary values to zero? And does stochastic rounding (NVFP4 SR) raise or lower NVFP4's SQNR?
blocks.reveal: E2M1 with one scale per tensor flushes **96.5%**: the scale is set by the 50s, so nearly everything else falls below FP4's 0.25 rounding threshold. Stochastic rounding **lowers** SQNR, from 16.3 to 13.7 dB: it removes bias but adds variance. That is why the NVFP4 recipe uses it only for gradients.

blocks.md:
The full output of part 4:

```

E2M1 tensor  MSE 0.89360  SQNR   0.5 dB  zeros  96.5%
MXFP4 down   MSE 0.04780  SQNR  13.6 dB  zeros  10.5%
MXFP4 up     MSE 0.04833  SQNR  13.5 dB  zeros  12.0%
NVFP4        MSE 0.02327  SQNR  16.3 dB  zeros   6.7%
NVFP4 SR     MSE 0.04237  SQNR  13.7 dB  zeros   6.7%
```

Block scaling recovers most of what per-tensor FP4 loses, and NVFP4 beats both MXFP4 rules by about 2.7 dB: its 16-value blocks hold fewer outlier-dominated values and its E4M3 scales land each block amax on 6.
